passage:
On the second Sunday of the month Usha took the train from her Pune flat to her parents' house. Over lunch her aunt said, "Why live alone when there's a room here?" Usha smiled and passed the salad. "Because I like my own place. But look at our whiteboard." On it, in Usha's handwriting: Usha pays the monthly grocery order and calls on odd days. Her brother Chaitanya handles the society meetings and bank visits and calls on even days. Wednesday evenings were Usha's pottery class, and nobody phoned then unless it mattered.
"We agreed this in March," Usha said. "If it gets heavy for anyone, we change it." Her father tapped the board and nodded, as if it were a contract everyone had signed.

qa.q: What day of the month did Usha visit her parents' house?
qa.a: Usha visited on the second Sunday of the month.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling when her aunt asked why she lived alone?
qa.a: She felt calm and sure of herself, shown by her smile and her explaining plainly that she likes her own place.

qa.q: What made Usha's arrangement fair to the whole family?
qa.a: The duties were agreed openly and split between Usha and her brother Chaitanya, with free evenings kept for Usha and a promise to change the plan if it gets heavy.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya see the whiteboard plan?
qa.a: Chaitanya likely finds it fair, since his tasks are written next to Usha's and the calls alternate on odd and even days.

grounding: A young adult supports family in agreed ways while keeping her own life, with duties freely chosen and fairly shared.

"Papa, I'm not saying this because I have to," said Lavanya, setting down the tea tray.
"I don't want you to feel bound," said Santosh.
"I feel chosen, not bound. I'll come every Saturday and take Amma to her walk in the park. Thursday evenings are for my pottery class. Those stay mine."
"And if the week is heavy?"
"Then I say so, and you don't sulk." She grinned.
"I never sulk," Santosh said.
"Papa."
"Fine, a little." He laughed. "And your brother?"
"Sunday lunch at his place, and he does the bank visits. I already asked him."
Amma called from the balcony, "Write it on the calendar so we all remember."
Lavanya took the marker.

qa.q: Which day did Lavanya say she would come every week?
qa.a: Lavanya said she would come every Saturday.

qa.q: What is Lavanya feeling about the duties she takes on?
qa.a: She feels chosen and willing, not bound, and also protective of her time, as she keeps Thursday evenings for pottery.

qa.q: What made the arrangement work for both Lavanya and her family?
qa.a: They agreed the days openly, kept her Thursday evenings, shared duties with her brother and said they would speak up if the week got heavy.

qa.q: Why might Santosh say he does not want Lavanya to feel bound?
qa.a: Santosh seems to want her help to be freely given and not an obligation, which is why he asks what happens if the week is heavy.

grounding: A young adult supports family in agreed ways while keeping her own time, and duty is freely chosen and fairly shared.

passage:
When Aai had her hip surgery last year, my sister Aditi and I nearly fell out. I'm Arohi; we're Aai and Baba's only two daughters. I live in Pune; she lives in Nagpur, near our parents. For months she'd done everything, and she was exhausted. I felt guilty, but also resentful when she said, "You only send money and think you've done your part."
So we did something we'd never done: we sat down with Aai and Baba and made a plan. Aditi handles weekday check-ins and doctor visits. I take the bills, the paperwork, and I come home one weekend a month so she gets a break. We agreed what I'd contribute and for how long. And I kept my job and my flat.
It's not perfect. But now nobody's keeping score. Aditi said last month, "I don't feel alone anymore." And I don't feel guilty for having my own life.

qa.q: Where does Aditi live?
qa.a: Aditi lives in Nagpur, near their parents.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Arohi have before the plan?
qa.a: Arohi felt guilty that Aditi was doing everything, but also resentful when Aditi said Arohi only sent money.

qa.q: What made the family's plan work?
qa.a: They sat down together and agreed on clear, fair roles, with each sister supporting in chosen ways while keeping her own life.

qa.q: How does Aditi feel after the plan?
qa.a: Aditi feels less alone and relieved, as she says she doesn't feel alone anymore.

grounding: A young adult and her sister agree openly how to share care for their parents, combining independence with freely chosen, fairly shared duty.

passage:
Family counselling note, session three.
Trisha, 26, and her husband Gurpreet came to discuss how to support both sets of parents without losing their own life together. His parents in Amritsar expect them to move back; her widowed mother in Kolkata lives alone.
Today they were calmer. Gurpreet said, "We can't move to both cities. But we can decide what each of us gives, clearly." They wrote a plan: one long visit to each city a year; a fixed day for calls to each parent; Trisha's brother agreed to check on her mother weekly; they will share his father's medical costs with his sister.
Trisha said, "For the first time, it feels like we chose this, not like it was forced on us." Gurpreet squeezed her hand.
Next step: they will present the plan to both families separately, and review it with me in three months.

qa.q: Where do Gurpreet's parents live?
qa.a: His parents live in Amritsar.

qa.q: What does Trisha's comment about choosing the plan suggest she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she feels relieved and more in control, because the duties now feel freely chosen instead of forced.

qa.q: What makes Trisha and Gurpreet's plan fair?
qa.a: They clearly divided visits, calls and shared costs with siblings, so support is freely chosen and fairly shared while they keep their life together.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet's parents feel about the plan?
qa.a: They may be disappointed that the couple won't move back, but reassured by regular visits and calls.

grounding: A counselling note shows a young couple supporting both sets of parents in clearly agreed ways while keeping their own life.

passage:
Sunday night
Big family meeting today. I've been living in Bengaluru for two years, sending money home whenever Papa asks, feeling guilty every time I buy something for myself. Hemant, my younger brother, has been at home doing everything for Dadi.
Today we finally talked like adults. Hemant said he wants to join a course in Pune next year. Papa said Dadi needs someone. I said I want to help, but I can't keep doing it without a plan.
We decided: I'll send a fixed amount every month for Dadi's care and Hemant's course fees, for two years. Hemant will arrange a day-helper for Dadi before he leaves. I'll visit every festival. And I'll keep my savings. Papa agreed, even to that part.
I feel lighter than I have in ages. It's still duty. But now it's a plan we chose together.
Kunal

qa.q: What does Hemant want to join next year?
qa.a: Hemant wants to join a course in Pune next year.

qa.q: How does Kunal feel after the family meeting?
qa.a: Kunal feels lighter and relieved, because the duty is now a plan chosen together instead of constant guilt.

qa.q: What made the family's decision fair?
qa.a: Everyone spoke openly, and they agreed who gives what and for how long, with Kunal keeping some savings and Hemant arranging help for Dadi.

qa.q: How might Hemant feel about the plan?
qa.a: Hemant would likely feel relieved and hopeful, since he can take his course while Dadi is still cared for.

grounding: A young adult and the family agree openly on how the support works and for how long, turning duty into freely chosen interdependence.
